_about: Audited record of where the catalog's factual claims come from. Keyed by 'module::cls', one entry per item, one record per claim. Fields: kind (credit = the attribution line the cabinet and the Field Guide show; data = figures or tables typed or generated from somewhere else; experiment = a result of our own); claim (what the cabinet asserts TODAY); verdict (correct | imprecise | wrong | not_an_attribution | unverifiable); source + url (the citation that was actually fetched, not recalled); proposed_claim (what the line should read — a PROPOSAL, not applied to the code); code_matches + code_note (whether the implementation is the thing being credited); ruling (the adversarial checker's reasoning); checked (ISO date a source was read against what ships; null = still unverified). Edit this file, then run tools/build_sources.py to regenerate SOURCES.md.
_coverage: Seeded 2026-09-22 from the 56 catalog entries that carry a 'credit', plus 6 items whose data comes from outside the repo and which carry no credit at all. Extended 2026-09-24 with 5 data-provenance entries for items that assert nothing checkable in a credit field but whose data tables come from identifiable traditions. Not covered: the 236 paintings and 70 wondercabinet titles (their provenance is in the gallery data, not in code), the 48 demos (they replay their game's own claims), and every item that asserts nothing checkable.

claims.source: M. Gerhardt and H. Schuster, "A cellular automaton describing the formation of spatially ordered structures in chemical systems", Physica D: Nonlinear Phenomena 36(3):209-221, August 1989, DOI 10.1016/0167-2789(89)90081-X. Named and popularised by A. K. Dewdney, "Computer Recreations: The hodgepodge machine makes waves", Scientific American 259(2), August 1988, pp. 104-107 (JSTOR stable 24989205).
claims.code_note: visuals/hodge.py:183 step_ca(). Healthy rule matches the published one exactly: new = (infected//k1) + (ill//k2), capped at n (Dewdney's [A/k1]+[B/k2]). Ill (state n) -> 0 matches. The INFECTED rule deviates: the code does `avg = total // 9; new = avg + int(g)`, i.e. it divides the 9-cell neighbourhood sum by a fixed 9. Both Dewdney's Scientific American statement ("dividing S ... by A, the number of infected neighbours") and Reiter's J implementation (`forinf =: 1: <. avg@inf + c`, the average over the INFECTED cells only) divide by the count of infected cells, not by 9. So this is a Gerhardt-Schuster-flavoured variant, not the published rule; with mostly-healthy neighbourhoods the fixed /9 systematically under-estimates the infection level. Also g is truncated with int(), so the 0.25-step g control only bites at integer boundaries. Everything else (states 0..n=63, Moore neighbourhood, toroidal wrap, synchronous double-buffer) is faithful.
claims.ruling: Re-fetched both sources myself. Crossref/Elsevier metadata returns exactly M. Gerhardt, H. Schuster, Physica D 36(3):209-221, 1989-08 — not reconstructed. I re-downloaded the Dewdney PDF and ran pdftotext on it rather than trusting the researcher's summary; the JSTOR header line reads "A. K. Dewdney / Scientific American, Vol. 259, No. 2 (AUGUST 1988), pp. 104-107" and the body says "the hodgepodge machine's creators, Martin Gerhardt and Heike Schuster of the University of Bielefeld in West Germany". So names, venue, year all hold and the credit names the originators, not the populariser — the right choice. I independently confirmed the code deviation the researcher found: visuals/hodge.py:216 step_ca() computes `total` as self+8 neighbours then `avg = total // 9`, whereas Dewdney's text states the degree of infection is "the sum of the state numbers of the cell and of its neighbors, by A, the number of infected neighbors" giving [S/A]+g, and Reiter's J code (fetched and text-extracted from webbox.lafayette.edu) defines `inf=: #~ ~:&0 *. ~:&1` / `avg=: +/ % #` / `forinf=: 1: <. avg@inf + c`, i.e. the mean over infected cells only. The healthy rule ((infected//k1)+(ill//k2), capped at n) and the ill->0 rule do match Dewdney verbatim. Verdict imprecise (missing year) upheld. One thing I would add: because the infected rule is not the published one, "After Gerhardt & Schuster, 1989" is the honest line unless the /9 divisor is fixed.

claims.source: Robert Axelrod, The Evolution of Cooperation, Basic Books, New York, 1984 — Chapter 8 contains the territorial (spatial-grid) iterated Prisoner's Dilemma. Described in Martin A. Nowak & Karl Sigmund, "Games on Grids", in U. Dieckmann, R. Law & J.A.J. Metz (eds.), The Geometry of Ecological Interactions: Simplifying Spatial Complexity, Cambridge University Press, 2000, pp. 135-150
claims.code_note: The strategy repertoire is Axelrod's (Always Cooperate / Always Defect / Tit-for-Tat / Random, with T>R>P>S payoffs R=3, T=5, S=0, P=1), but the simulation the panel shows is not Axelrod's. _step() plays every cell against its 8 Moore neighbours, sums payoffs, then in "Phase 2: Each cell adopts strategy of highest-scoring in neighborhood" — that imitate-the-best-neighbour update on a 2D lattice is precisely the Nowak & May 1992 spatial game, published eight years after the credited book. Axelrod 1984 was a non-spatial round-robin computer tournament, not a grid. So the name on screen belongs to the strategies, while the thing being animated belongs to someone else.
claims.ruling: Overturned. The ruling's load-bearing claim — "Axelrod 1984 was a non-spatial round-robin computer tournament, not a grid" — is simply false, and it drove a wrong correction. Nowak & Sigmund's own survey chapter states it plainly (pp. 136-137, text I extracted from the PDF): "In Chapter 8 of his book, Axelrod describes an iterated Prisoner's Dilemma game played on a spatial grid. He considers a territory subdivided into square cells, with each cell occupied by one player. Each player plays against his or her four neighbors in a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma game. The total scores are computed. If a player has neighbors who are more successful, he or she switches to the strategy that obtained the highest score." That is exactly _step() in visuals/gametheory.py: Phase 1 sums payoffs against the neighbourhood, Phase 2 adopts the highest-scoring neighbour's strategy. The same chapter identifies what was actually new in Nowak & May 1992: the ONE-SHOT game — "cooperators can persist even if there is no retribution, that is, even if the game is never repeated" — with only unconditional C and D. The code is the opposite of that: it is the ITERATED game with memory (last_action, TIT_FOR_TAT returning the neighbour's last action at line 164-166) and Axelrod's tournament payoffs R=3, T=5, S=0, P=1, not Nowak & May's degenerate matrix. So "Robert Axelrod, 1984" is the correct credit and the GUIDE desc "Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma tournament on a spatial grid" is accurate; the proposed "Axelrod 1984; Nowak & May 1992" would have added a citation for something the code does not do. Only divergences from Axelrod's own version are cosmetic and covered by the same chapter as immaterial: MOORE 8 neighbours instead of his 4, and 4 strategies instead of the tournament field. Axelrod 1984/Basic Books confirmed from that chapter's reference list ("Axelrod R (1984). The Evolution of Cooperation. New York, NY, USA: Basic Books") and Open Library (first_publish_year 1984). Two side notes survive, both outside the credit line: the legend 'TFT' says the preset "starts with half the grid cooperating, half defecting" but MIXES[3] is ("TFT vs DEFECT", 0.00 coop, 0.50 defect, 0.50 TFT) — I confirmed this in the source, and the legend needs fixing; and the claim that Tit-for-Tat was submitted to Axelrod by Anatol Rapoport is plausible but I did not verify it this session, so it should not be written anywhere as fact yet.

So even the Axelrod half credits the organiser/populariser rather than the originator of the strategy — acceptable for a credit line, but the GUIDE desc says "tournament", which is the Axelrod frame, while the pixels show the Nowak-May frame. claims.source: Science Museum Group Collection, object co1031, "Early pendulum clock by Salomon Coster, c.1657": "The Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens (1629-1693) made the first successful pendulum clock in December 1656 and in the following year he granted Coster the sole right to make them."
